title: Chrysippus
author: Ancient
content:
Chrysippus
 

"He alone is the sage, the others only act as shadows."
 

Ancient saying cited in 
Les Stoïciens: textes choisis
 par
Jean Brun ,Press Universitaires de France, 1973
 

(280 BC - 206 BC), Chrysippus was the greatest of the Greek Stoic philosophers and is
considered to be an equal to Aristotle, particularly concerning logic. Born in Assos,
Troade, he was probably of Phoenician roots. It is believed that he was a former pupil of
Cleanthe or Zeno. He eventually took over the Athenian Stoa academy . Together with Zeno,
he is considered the cofounder of Stoicism. 

He was a prolific but apparently disorganized writer, often writing continuously on the
same subject and jotting down everything that came to mind. He made innumerable
corrections and made prolific use of citations. It is said that at one stage he even
quoted a long work of Euripides in its entirety! In all, he is credited with over 750
writings, none of which are extant. It was said that, "Without Chrysippus, there
wouldn't have been any Stoicism" 

He was a celebrated dialectician of his time. He was held in such high esteem that it
was said that if the gods made the dialectic then it was to serve for no other than
Chrysippus 

Chrysippus was among the first to organize propositional logic as an intellectual
discipline. He formalized many of the intuitive principles of Stoicism. He defended,
against the Megarian logicians and the Skeptics, the fundamental Stoic principle regarding
certain knowledge, the comprehensive presentation, proposition and argument, criterions of
truth and 
assent
. Possibly one of his greatest achievements can be seen in his
"five undemonstrable syllogisms" which provide the logical foundations of the
Stoic system. There has been a renewal of interest in the subtleties of Stoic logic over
recent times.. 

With great energy and diligence he accomplished a complete overhaul of the themes in
logic, physics and ethics developed earlier by Zeno. In physics, Chrysippus was
responsible for refining the subtle relationships between fate and free will, a
fundamental aspect of Stoic thought. He clarified distinctions between "whole"
and "all," or "universe," and argued that the whole is the world,
while the all is the external void together with the world. 

He expanded Zeno's cosmology where the origin of man was seen as providentially being
generated by "fiery reason" out of matter. Chrysippus also incorporated the
concept of self-preservation as a governing principle of all living things. The
qualification to living things may not even have been a limitation as a popular concept
amongst many Stoics - as expounded by Cleanthe - was that all was part and parcel of a
living totality. 

Chrysippus developed the distinction between world nature and human nature. This leads
to the fundamental moral principle of good being based on acting in accord with both human
and universal nature. (see Epictetus 
The
Discourses
, for some practical explanations) The rather eclectic and piecemeal
approach that characterize much of modern thought seems to lead to an interpretation of
this principle as being "yet another notion of good" that is reserved for
students of specialised courses in ethics. However, the same principle underlies the whole
Stoic system in physics and logic as well. For Chrysippus it would have been a seminal
logical principle exploited over and over again in the development and exposition of the
total Stoic system. 

To illustrate what is meant here, refer to the long running debate in quantum
  mechanics concerning whether the laws of physics can be expressed as an extrapolation of
  the physics of localized phenomena. Findings by Bell seem to indicate the contrary and
  that there are seemingly mysterious non-localized phenomena acting instantaneously over
  vast distances. Chrysippus's logical principles could offer new and profound insights into
  this vexing question. One could say that the principles apply to the logical
  interrelationships between the generic individual and its equally generic environment.
  Such a theory can "assent" to the human individual or the photon - it all
  depends on context and the nature of the individual in question. Overall, the system must
  be in harmony. To use a modern term, the constituents in the system "must
  commute" in some way. Chrysippus seemed to have an understanding of how this all
  works. 

There are several anecdotes about the death of Chrysippus. One story is that his
disciples invited him to a sacrifice during the time that he philosophized at the Odeon.
He drank some over proof wine and fainted, dying five hours later at the age of 73.
Another version is that he died of laughter. Seeing an ass eating at some figs, he
suggested to the old woman who owned the ass to give it a glass of wine. He then broke
into a fit of laughter that ended up killing him. 

Of passing interest is to note that none of the many works that he wrote were ever
dedicated to a king, which was contrary to the custom of the times. 

It is said that Chrysippus covered almost every feature of Stoic doctrine and treated
each so thoroughly and exhaustively that the essential features of the Stoic school were
to remain virtually unchanged after his time..
